chapter: Chapter 8 — France and the Fur Trade
title: France and the Fur Trade — The Age of Exploration, Chapter 8
eyebrow: CKHG Grade 5 · The Age of Exploration · Chapter 8 · Student Reader pp. 66–73
bigQuestion: The French and the English had different approaches to settlement in North America. In what ways were they different?

missions.name: France and the Fur Trade
missions.blurb: One quiz for the whole chapter, with questions from each of its four headed sections and the Big Question at the end. Mostly what happened; a few on the words the chapter is built from. The card says which page answers it, and a wrong answer opens that page.

hi: did not want to be left behind
a cartographer, sailed with him

vs.q: Why did King Francis I of France send out an expedition in 1524?
opts: He did not want France to be left behind
He had been promised a share of the spice trade
He wanted to attack the Spanish colonies
He had been asked to by the pope in Rome
vs.why: Spain was mining gold and silver in Mexico and Peru, Portugal ruled the spice trade, and England had already sent Cabot looking for the Northwest Passage. France had nothing.

vs.q: Verrazano's brother was a cartographer. What is a cartographer?
opts: A mapmaker
A ship's doctor
A fur trader
A translator
vs.why: North America had not been mapped by Europeans, and one goal of the expedition was accurate maps of the Atlantic coast. You take a mapmaker along for that.

hi: the first European to sail up the Atlantic coast
it was a deep-water harbor

vs.q: What was Verrazano the first European to do?
opts: Sail up the Atlantic coast of what is now the United States
Reach the Mississippi River from the north
Sail all the way round the whole island of Newfoundland
Build a French settlement on the St. Lawrence
vs.why: From North Carolina up to Newfoundland. He never got home — he was killed on an island in the Caribbean.

vs.q: What did Verrazano notice about New York Bay?
opts: It was a deep-water harbor
It froze over every winter
It was the mouth of a great river
It had no safe place to anchor
vs.why: A deep-water harbor is one big ships can use. The entrance to New York Harbor is spanned today by the Verrazano-Narrows Bridge, named for him.

hi: a rich fishing ground
the mouth of a mighty river

vs.q: What did Cartier find off the coast of Newfoundland in 1534?
opts: English and Spanish fishing fleets
A French colony already settled there
The entrance to the Northwest Passage
A Native American village on an island
vs.why: The waters there were a rich fishing ground, and other countries had got there first. Those fisheries matter later — they are how the fur trade starts.

vs.q: What did Cartier fail to realise about the Gulf of St. Lawrence?
opts: It was the mouth of a mighty river
It was already claimed by England
It was frozen for half the year
It was not connected to the sea
vs.why: He claimed the land around the gulf and went home. He came back a year later and sailed up the river he had missed.

hi: He climbed a hill and named it Mount Royal
taught the French how to brew a drink made from evergreen trees

vs.q: Cartier climbed a hill and named it Mount Royal. What is on that site today?
opts: The Canadian city of Montreal
The Canadian city of Quebec
The American city of New York
The port of St. John's
vs.why: Mount Royal, Montreal. He had sailed up the St. Lawrence and visited a Native American village on an island in the river.

vs.q: What saved Cartier's men when they fell sick with scurvy?
opts: A drink brewed from evergreen trees
Supplies that arrived from France
Moving the camp farther south
Fish caught through holes in the ice
vs.why: Native Americans taught them how to make it, and it cured them. We now know such a brew is rich in vitamin C, which is exactly what scurvy is a lack of.

hi: the king released prisoners from jail
That colony was doomed from the start

vs.q: How did the French king try to find settlers for his colony?
opts: He released prisoners from jail and sent them
He paid farming families to cross the Atlantic
He ordered his soldiers to stay and settle
He invited settlers from England and Spain
vs.why: French people could not easily be persuaded to settle in a cold, distant land. So the king emptied some jails instead.

vs.q: Why was that colony doomed from the start?
opts: The settlers would not work, and supplies came late
The land turned out to be owned by England
A disease killed most of the settlers
The king changed his mind and recalled them all
vs.why: The prisoners were happy to be out of jail but not eager to work in such difficult conditions. Cartier gave up and went home, and France ignored the land for sixty years.

hi: The French wanted to trade furs, particularly beaver skins
in great demand in Europe for making men's hats

vs.q: What did the French want from the Native Americans?
opts: Furs, especially beaver skins
Gold and silver from inland mines
Land for building large farms
Timber for building ships
vs.why: Beaver above all. This is the trade the whole chapter is named for, and it grew out of French fishing boats off Newfoundland.

vs.q: Why were beaver skins in such demand in Europe?
opts: They were used for making men's hats
They were used to line winter boots
They were burned as a kind of fuel
They were used to make writing paper
vs.why: Hats. An entire North American empire grew out of what was fashionable on European heads.

hi: eager to have tools and other metal goods
an explorer named Samuel de Champlain

vs.q: What did the Native Americans want in exchange?
opts: Tools and other metal goods
Horses and cattle
Guns and gunpowder
Cloth and glass beads
vs.why: Metal goods. Trade relationships grew slowly, out of French fishermen meeting local people on the same coast year after year.

vs.q: Who was the key figure in the settlement of New France?
opts: Samuel de Champlain
Jacques Cartier
Giovanni da Verrazano
Louis Jolliet
vs.why: Champlain. The fur trade made colonies worth having, and he is the one who built them.

hi: Farming was difficult because the growing season was so short
moved the settlement to the site of Quebec City

vs.q: Farming was hard in New France because the growing season was short. What is a growing season?
opts: The days in a year for planting and harvesting
The months when a river is free of ice
The time it takes a single crop to ripen
The part of the year when furs are best
vs.why: How many days a year you can actually farm. With long hard winters there were not many, which is a large part of why so few settlers came.

vs.q: Where did Champlain move his settlement in 1608?
opts: To the site of Quebec City
To the island of Montreal
To the coast of Maine
To the Gulf of Mexico
vs.why: On the banks of the St. Lawrence, at a point where the river narrows, with the town built on the heights looking over the water.

hi: At first very few settlers came to New France
Champlain sailed to New France for the first time

vs.q: Why did very few settlers come to New France at first?
opts: The winters were long and farming was hard
The king would not allow families to go
The Native Americans drove them out
There was no way to make any money there
vs.why: Long hard winters and a short growing season. New France grew quite differently from the English colonies to the south.

vs.q: When did Champlain first sail to New France?
vs.why: 1603, exploring the coasts of Maine and Nova Scotia, where he founded his first settlement before moving it to Quebec five years later.

hi: Fur traders canoed and portaged farther and farther
an expedition led by Jacques Marquette

vs.q: Fur traders canoed and portaged into the wilderness. What does portage mean?
opts: To carry boats and supplies overland
To paddle upstream against a current
To trade goods at a riverside post
To map a river from its mouth upward
vs.why: Carrying the canoe between one waterway and the next. It is how the fur trade pushed deeper into North America than any map went.

vs.q: Which expedition first reached the Mississippi River, and when?
opts: Marquette and Jolliet, in 1673
Cartier and Champlain, in 1608
La Salle and Verrazano, in 1524
Champlain and Jolliet, in 1603
vs.why: The first European expedition to get there, and it got there because of furs. Exploration followed the trade, not the other way round.

hi: claimed all the land drained by the Mississippi
a sizable empire with hardly any settlers

vs.q: What did La Salle claim for the king of France in 1682?
opts: All the land drained by the Mississippi
Every island in the Gulf of Mexico
The whole of the St. Lawrence valley
The fisheries off Newfoundland
vs.why: He sailed the Mississippi down to the Gulf of Mexico and claimed everything its waters touched — an enormous claim made by one man in a boat.

vs.q: By 1700, what was strange about New France?
opts: It was a huge empire with hardly any settlers
It had more settlers than the English colonies
It had been handed over to England
It had no trade with Europe at all
vs.why: About ten thousand Europeans in the whole of it. Compare that with the English colonies filling up the Atlantic coast, and the Big Question answers itself.

hi: English colonists forcefully pushed Native Americans off land
had focused on trade

vs.q: In what ways were the French and English approaches to settlement different?
opts: The French came to trade; the English came to take land
The French came to farm; the English came to fish
The French sent soldiers; the English sent priests
The French built cities; the English built forts
vs.why: This is the chapter's Big Question. English colonists forcefully pushed Native Americans off land they had lived on for generations. The French had not tried to conquer them, but had focused on trade.

vs.q: What kind of people mostly settled in New France?
opts: Rugged adventurers, and not many of them
Whole families looking for farmland
Soldiers sent out by the French king
Fishermen who stayed on after the season
vs.why: That suited the French government for a while: the colony made a profit and its few settlers needed little supervision. The English colonies filled up with families instead, which is the other half of the difference.

joins.title: France Joins In — late to the race
text: In the early 1500s, Spain was mining gold and silver in Mexico and Peru. Portugal ruled the spice trade in the Indian Ocean. England had sent John Cabot to look for the Northwest Passage. The king of France, Francis I, did not want to be left behind.

Verrazano's brother, a cartographer, sailed with him. North America was new to the Europeans and had not been mapped. One of the goals of Verrazano's expedition was to create accurate maps of the Atlantic coast.

verrazano.title: France Joins In — Verrazano's coast
text: Verrazano was the first European to sail up the Atlantic coast of the present-day United States, from North Carolina to Newfoundland. When he sailed into New York Bay, he noted that it was a deep-water harbor. Today the entrance to New York Harbor is spanned by the Verrazano-Narrows Bridge, named in his honor.
Verrazano did not make it back to Europe. He was killed on an island in the Caribbean.

cartier.title: Jacques Cartier — the river he sailed past
text: In 1534 France's king asked Jacques Cartier, a French sea captain, to explore the coast of North America. Cartier sailed to Newfoundland, where he encountered English and Spanish fishing fleets. This area of water off the coast of Newfoundland was a rich fishing ground.

Cartier continued his voyage, exploring the coast of Labrador and the Gulf of St. Lawrence. At the time, Cartier did not realize that the Gulf of St. Lawrence was in fact the mouth of a mighty river. Instead of exploring further, he claimed the land around the gulf for France and returned to Europe.

scurvy.title: Jacques Cartier — a hard winter, and a cure
text: Cartier visited a Native American village on an island in the St. Lawrence. He climbed a hill and named it Mount Royal. This site eventually became part of the Canadian city of Montreal.
During the winter, Cartier's men became sick with scurvy. The snow was four-feet deep. Many of Cartier's men died from the cold and sickness. Cartier gave up hope of ever returning to France.

The friendship between Cartier and the Native Americans saved him and his men. The Native Americans taught the French how to brew a drink made from evergreen trees. (Today we know that such a brew is rich in vitamin C.) It cured the French explorers of their scurvy.

prisoners.title: Jacques Cartier — a colony made of prisoners
text: Cartier returned on a third voyage to what is now Canada. The French king wanted a colony in North America. But French people could not be easily persuaded to become settlers in this cold, distant land. Instead, the king released prisoners from jail and sent them to settle in North America.

That colony was doomed from the start. The prisoners were happy to get out of jail but not eager to work in such difficult conditions. Supply ships were late in arriving. Jacques Cartier was forced to give up and return to France.

fur.title: Champlain and New France — where the fur trade came from
text: During the 1500s, French ships did venture to the waters off Newfoundland to fish. As a result, trade relationships slowly developed between the French fishermen and the local Native Americans. The Native Americans were eager to have tools and other metal goods. The French wanted to trade furs, particularly beaver skins, which were in great demand in Europe for making men's hats.

The development of a fur trade in North America led to a renewed effort by the French to establish colonies in the land they called New France. The key figure in the settlement of New France was an explorer named Samuel de Champlain.

quebec.title: Champlain and New France — Quebec, and a short summer
vocab: the days available in a year to plant and harvest crops
text: In 1603, Champlain sailed to New France for the first time. He explored the coast of Maine and Nova Scotia. He founded his first settlement in Nova Scotia. In 1608, Champlain moved the settlement to the site of Quebec City, on the banks of the St. Lawrence River. At a point where the river narrows, Champlain built a town on the heights with a view of the river.
New France grew differently than the English colonies. At first very few settlers came to New France. The winters were long and hard. Farming was difficult because the growing season was so short.

differently.title: Champlain and New France — trade instead of conquest
vocab: to carry boats and supplies overland from one waterway to another
text: Those who did settle in New France were mostly rugged adventurers. For a while that suited the French government. The colony made a profit, and for the most part the colony's few settlers did not need a great deal of supervision.

It is probably true to say that the settlers in New France also dealt with the Native Americans living nearby somewhat differently than the English did in the colonies to the south. English colonists forcefully pushed Native Americans off land they had lived on for generations. In New France, the relationship between the fur traders and the Native American tribes was more peaceful. The French had not tried to conquer the Native Americans, but instead had focused on trade.
The fur trade also resulted in further exploration. Fur traders canoed and portaged farther and farther into the North American wilderness. In 1673, an expedition led by Jacques Marquette

lasalle.title: The Mississippi River — an empire with nobody in it
text: La Salle claimed all the land drained by the Mississippi for the king of France.
By 1700, New France was a sizable empire with hardly any settlers. There were only about ten thousand Europeans in the entire area.
